ball.q: Chris Kirkland's father put a bet on with William Hill at 100-1 when Chris was a boy, and collected nearly 10,000 pounds in 2006. What was the bet?
ball.a: That his son would play for England

ball.q: Europe had an international club competition from 1927, decades before the European Cup. What was it called?
ball.a: The Mitropa Cup, Hugo Meisl's idea

ball.q: The 1909 Scottish Cup was never awarded to anyone. What went wrong?
ball.a: Both games were drawn, fans rioted over the lack of extra time and the clubs refused to play a third

ball.q: Fourteen players were arrested over Italy's 1980 Totonero betting scandal. What made the arrests so public?
ball.a: They were taken in at the grounds on a live Serie A matchday, some straight off the pitch

ball.q: Who is the pipe-smoking sailor on Sampdoria's shirt?
ball.a: Baciccia, the Genoese form of Giovanni Battista

ball.q: The goalkeeper who saved four penalties in the 1986 European Cup final shootout never played for Steaua again. Why not?
ball.a: A blood clot in his arm that summer ended his top-level career

ball.q: The Intertoto Cup was set up in 1961 to serve an industry rather than the supporters. Which industry?
ball.a: The football pools, so betting coupons had fixtures through the summer

ball.q: Accrington Stanley resigned from the Football League in March 1962 with 13 matches still to play, then changed their minds. How quickly?
ball.a: Three days later, but the League held them to the first letter

ball.q: Bohemians Prague are nicknamed the Kangaroos and carry one on the badge. Why?
ball.a: They were given two live kangaroos after touring Australia in 1927, and handed them to Prague Zoo

ball.q: France's oldest club plays in sky blue and navy, the colours of two English universities. Which club, and which universities?
ball.a: Le Havre, in the colours of Oxford and Cambridge

ball.q: In September 1946 England played two different sides both called Ireland within three days. What did Johnny Carey and Bill Gorman manage?
ball.a: They played for both of them

ball.q: Penarol's founding club of 1891 was named for cricket and for the employer whose staff set it up. Which employer?
ball.a: The Central Uruguay Railway

ball.q: Guruceta gave Real Madrid a penalty for a foul outside the box at Camp Nou in 1970. What had the crowd covered the pitch with?
ball.a: Seat cushions

ball.q: Racing Santander's players took the field for a 2014 Copa del Rey tie and refused to kick off. What were they protesting about?
ball.a: Months of unpaid wages, they wanted the board out

ball.q: After signing John Aldridge in 1989, Real Sociedad ran an odd compromise policy until 2001. What was it?
ball.a: They would sign Basques and foreigners, but no other Spaniards

ball.q: Barcelona top scorer Quini was taken at gunpoint in March 1981 and the title challenge fell apart. How long was he held?
ball.a: 25 days

ball.q: Barcelona took the Salvadoran genius Mágico González on a pre-season tour of the United States in 1984. How did it end?
ball.a: Menotti sent him back to Cádiz and the transfer never happened

ball.q: The touring Basque side of the Civil War settled abroad and entered the local league for 1938-39. Which country was it?
ball.a: Mexico, where they finished second as CD Euzkadi

ball.q: El Salvador lost 10-1 to Hungary at Elche in 1982 with only 20 men in a 22 man squad. Where had the other two places gone?
ball.a: To government officials who wanted a trip to Europe

ball.q: UD Las Palmas moved into the Estadio Insular the year they were founded without building it. Which club had opened it in 1944?
ball.a: Marino FC

ball.q: For its first seven years the Estadio Insular had a pitch no La Liga club would accept today. What was it?
ball.a: Dirt, grass was only laid in 1951

ball.q: Real Madrid's 1966 European Cup winners are known as the Yé-yé side. Where did the name come from?
ball.a: The Beatles, after four players posed as them for a Marca photo

ball.q: Racing Club's long title drought was blamed on something Independiente fans were said to have buried under the pitch. What was it?
ball.a: Seven dead cats

ball.q: Colo-Colo have carried a black band on the crest since 1927. Who is it mourning?
ball.a: Founder David Arellano, who died in Valladolid on the club's Spanish tour

ball.q: Brazil ditched the white shirt after the Maracanazo and picked the yellow one through a newspaper competition in 1953. Who won it?
ball.a: Aldyr Schlee, a teenager from Rio Grande do Sul

ball.q: Argentina boasted they had everything while bidding for the 1962 World Cup. What was Chile's Carlos Dittborn's famous reply?
ball.a: Because we have nothing, we will do everything

ball.q: Carlos Dittborn won Chile the 1962 World Cup and rebuilt the country to hold it, but never saw a match. Why not?
ball.a: He died about a month before it started

ball.q: Three Estudiantes players were jailed for 30 days after the brutal 1969 Intercontinental Cup second leg against Milan. Who ordered it?
ball.a: Argentina's military ruler, President Juan Carlos Onganía

ball.q: Chile's keeper Roberto Rojas went down bleeding when a flare landed near him at the Maracanã in 1989. What did the investigation find?
ball.a: The flare had missed him and he had cut himself with a blade

ball.q: What did Chile lose as punishment for the Roberto Rojas fake injury in 1989?
ball.a: The 1994 World Cup, they were barred from even entering qualifying

ball.q: Rio's grand clubs told Vasco da Gama in 1924 to drop twelve players because they were black or working class. What did Vasco do?
ball.a: Refused, in a letter known as the Historical Response, and took being shut out of the elite league

ball.q: Honduras were flown into the 2001 Copa América to replace Argentina, arriving hours before their first game. How far did they get?
ball.a: Third place, beating holders Brazil 2-0 in the quarter-final

ball.q: Football's deadliest disaster happened at the Estadio Nacional in Lima in 1964, with 328 killed. What set it off?
ball.a: The referee disallowing a late Peru equaliser against Argentina

ball.q: Carlos Henrique Raposo, known as Kaiser, was signed through the 1980s by Botafogo, Flamengo, Fluminense and Vasco. What did he never do?
ball.a: Play a competitive match, he faked injuries and fitness the whole time

ball.q: When FIFA banned internationals above 2,500 metres in 2007, Diego Maradona played an exhibition in La Paz in protest. Who led the team against him?
ball.a: Bolivia's president Evo Morales

ball.q: Palmeiras were called Palestra Itália until the Brazilian government forced a change in 1942. Why?
ball.a: Brazil had joined the Allies and banned names linked to the Axis powers

ball.q: River Plate blew a 2-0 lead in the 1966 Libertadores final play-off. What did rival fans throw at them days later, giving River a nickname that stuck?
ball.a: A chicken, painted with a red sash

ball.q: Alcides Ghiggia, who scored the winner in the 1950 Maracanazo, said only three people had ever silenced the Maracanã. Who were the other two?
ball.a: The Pope and Frank Sinatra

ball.q: René Higuita spent seven months in a Colombian jail in 1993 and missed the World Cup. What had he done?
ball.a: Acted as a go between in a kidnapping and taken money for it, which was illegal

ball.q: Spain’s oldest club was founded in 1889 by two Scottish doctors working at the Rio Tinto mines. Which club?
ball.a: Recreativo de Huelva

ball.q: Argentinos Juniors, the club that produced Maradona, grew out of two anarchist teams in 1904. One was named after which martyrs?
ball.a: The Chicago martyrs of the Haymarket affair

ball.q: Joe Gaetjens scored the goal that beat England at the 1950 World Cup. What happened to him in Haiti in 1964?
ball.a: Duvalier's secret police arrested him and he was never seen again

ball.q: Haiti's Emmanuel Sanon scored past Dino Zoff at the 1974 World Cup and ended a record that still stands. What record?
ball.a: Zoff had gone over 1,100 minutes of international football without conceding

ball.q: Ethiopia reached the final of the first Africa Cup of Nations in 1957 without playing a match. How?
ball.a: Four entered, South Africa were thrown out for refusing a mixed race side, so Ethiopia had a bye

ball.q: Referee Janny Sikazwe blew full time twice too early in Tunisia against Mali at the January 2022 Africa Cup of Nations. What was the given reason?
ball.a: Heatstroke and severe dehydration

ball.q: Ghana's team are the Black Stars after a symbol borrowed from a Pan-Africanist's shipping line. Whose line was it?
ball.a: Marcus Garvey's Black Star Line

ball.q: Two countries got to keep an Africa Cup of Nations trophy outright by winning it three times. Ghana in 1978 and who in 2000?
ball.a: Cameroon

ball.q: Nigeria pulled out of the 1996 Africa Cup of Nations in South Africa on the orders of dictator Sani Abacha. What did it cost them?
ball.a: A ban from the next tournament, in 1998

ball.q: Uzbekistan beat Bahrain 1-0 in a 2006 World Cup play-off, complained about the referee and had the result annulled. How did that work out?
ball.a: The replay finished 1-1, the second leg 0-0, and Bahrain went through on away goals

ball.q: The Dutch East Indies played at the 1938 World Cup and hold a record no one has taken off them. What record?
ball.a: The shortest World Cup history of any nation, one match, a 6-0 loss to Hungary

ball.q: India qualified for the 1950 World Cup and withdrew. Legend says FIFA banned their bare feet, but what reason did the federation give?
ball.a: Team selection disputes and not enough time to prepare

ball.q: Timor-Leste were banned from the 2023 Asian Cup back in 2017 and had 29 results wiped. What had they been doing?
ball.a: Fielding Brazilian born players on faked Timorese birth documents

ball.q: Belenenses started a 2021 league game against Benfica with nine players after a Covid outbreak. Why was it abandoned early in the second half?
ball.a: They were down to six on the pitch, below the minimum of seven
